chapters.title: Chapter 3: India's Sovereign Debt Sustainability, Examined

lessons.title: Stress-Testing India: Is the Debt Path Actually Sustainable?

body.text: Run India's own numbers through this course's own identity, and the debt path holds up comfortably under normal conditions, and comes uncomfortably close to the IMF's own disputed adverse scenario once growth and rates move against it at the same time. Sustainability was never really about the headline ratio. It was about the range either side of it.

children.text: This lesson does not introduce a new framework. It applies every tool this course has already built, the debt dynamics identity, the standard DSA stress-test shocks, the fiscal reaction function evidence, and the market's own pricing, directly to India, using the numbers already established across the previous seven lessons. If you have been reading straight through, you already have every input this lesson needs.

body.text: The combined shock scenario, a sustained growth slowdown paired with a sustained rise in borrowing costs, lands at roughly 99% of GDP after five years, remarkably close to the roughly 100% of GDP figure the IMF's own 2024 Article IV adverse scenario for India reportedly produced (Chapter 1, Lesson 2), the projection India's government publicly disputed. That is not a coincidence; it reflects the same underlying mechanism at a similar order of magnitude. The real disagreement in that episode was never about the arithmetic. It was about how likely a shock of this specific size and persistence actually is, exactly the kind of judgment call this course has repeatedly shown sits behind every headline sustainability number.

None of these scenarios are forecasts. They are stylised illustrations built from approximate figures established earlier in this course, using round, constant shock sizes for clarity. A real DSA uses actual historical volatility, country-specific calibration, and updated data; treat this exercise as a demonstration of the method, not a prediction of India's actual debt path.

children.text: What the Fiscal Reaction Function Adds to This Picture

Chapter 1, Lesson 3 found India's own fiscal reaction function to be modestly positive at the central government level, meaning the primary balance has historically improved somewhat as debt rises, but considerably weaker and more procyclical at the state level. Applied to the stress scenarios above, this matters directly: if debt actually starts climbing the way the growth-shock or combined-shock paths show, the empirical evidence gives only modest confidence that discretionary policy alone would deliver enough correction to arrest it. That is precisely the gap the FRBM Act's debt-anchored glide path, covered in the previous lesson, is meant to fill by legislating a target rather than relying on discretion. And it is precisely why the FRBM Act's own history of missed deadlines and stretched escape clauses matters here too: the backstop meant to catch a bad scenario has itself proven unreliable exactly when it has been tested hardest.
What the Market Is Actually Pricing: Reconciling Yields, CDS, and the Rating

None of the four stress scenarios above are what the market or the rating agencies are actually pricing into India today. India's 10-year G-Sec yield sits close to 7%, on an upward-sloping curve, nothing like the inverted, distress-priced curves covered in Chapter 2, Lesson 1. India's sovereign CDS, thin as it is, is not signalling acute stress. And two of the three major agencies moved India's outlook to positive, not negative, in 2024, the opposite direction from what a market bracing for a run toward 99% or 100% of GDP would show. Reconciling this with the stress test above is not a contradiction; it tells you the market's central expectation sits far closer to the baseline path than to the combined shock, and it should: India's r-g gap is currently favourable, its debt is overwhelmingly rupee-denominated and held domestically, the same structural point that let Japan sustain a far higher ratio in Chapter 1, Lesson 2's comparison table, and its contingent liabilities, while real, have so far been managed through disclosed, legislated mechanisms rather than surfacing as a surprise.

body.title: Textbook Distress Signals vs What India Actually Shows

columns.label: Textbook Signals of Sovereign Distress
points: Inverted yield curve, short yields far above long (Chapter 2, Lesson 1)
Sharply rising or already-elevated CDS spreads relative to peers (Chapter 2, Lesson 2)
Negative rating outlook or a recent downgrade, especially near the investment-grade line (Chapter 2, Lesson 3)
Contingent liabilities surfacing as a surprise rather than being tracked (Chapter 1, Lesson 2; Chapter 3, Lesson 1)
A flat or negative fiscal reaction function, no discretionary correction as debt rises (Chapter 1, Lesson 3)

columns.label: What India Actually Shows Today
points: An upward-sloping G-Sec curve, consistent with normal term compensation, not distress pricing
CDS liquidity thinner than peers, but not signalling acute stress, and used cautiously for exactly that reason
BBB-/Baa3 with a positive outlook from two of three major agencies as of 2024, the opposite direction from a distress signal
Known contingent liabilities (DISCOMs, NHAI, bank recapitalisation) tracked and periodically absorbed through legislated schemes like UDAY, not hidden until a crisis
A modest but positive fiscal reaction function at the central level, weaker at the state level, reinforced by the FRBM Act's debt-anchored glide path as a legislated backstop

children.text: The Actual Verdict: Where the Real Risk Sits

Put together, the honest answer to this lesson's title is neither a reassuring 'yes' nor an alarmed 'no'. India's baseline debt path is genuinely sustainable, resting on a real and currently favourable r-g gap, a debt stock insulated from foreign-currency rollover risk, and a fiscal rule that at least legislates a direction of travel even if its own history is imperfect. The real tail risk this chapter's tools point to is not the headline 82% ratio itself, and not any single one of Chapter 1's blind spots in isolation, growth optimism, a hidden liability, a missing correction, but several of them compounding at once: a sustained growth deceleration meeting a sustained rate shock meeting a contingent liability crystallising in the same window, the exact combination the combined and contingent-liability scenarios above were built to isolate. That compounding, not the ratio on its own, is the scenario actually worth underwriting against.

body.title: Write the Investment Committee Memo
body.scenario: Your fund's investment committee asks for a one-paragraph, evidence-based answer to: 'Is India's sovereign debt sustainable over the next five years?' You have this course's full toolkit available: the debt dynamics identity, DSA-style stress tests, the fiscal reaction function evidence, and the market's own pricing.
body.modelAnswer: Under baseline assumptions, a G-Sec yield near 7% against nominal growth near 9 to 10%, and a manageable primary deficit, India's general government debt-to-GDP ratio is on a gently declining path from roughly 82% today, consistent with both the market's own pricing (an upward-sloping yield curve, contained CDS, and a positive rating outlook from two of three major agencies) and India's structural insulation from foreign-currency rollover risk. The material risk is not this baseline; it is a scenario in which a sustained growth slowdown pushes the effective interest rate above nominal growth at the same time a contingent liability, most plausibly a DISCOM-style crystallisation or a banking-sector stress event, adds meaningfully to the debt stock, a combination that could push the ratio toward, though not conclusively past, the roughly 100% of GDP level flagged in the IMF's own disputed 2024 adverse scenario. Recommend monitoring the growth and interest rate trend closely, alongside state-level DISCOM and PSU-guarantee exposure, rather than the headline debt ratio in isolation.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Based on the stress test built in this lesson, which single shock, applied on its own, does the most damage to India's debt trajectory over five years?
options: The interest rate shock alone (r rising to 9%)
The combined shock, a sustained growth slowdown together with a sustained rise in interest rates
The one-off contingent liability shock alone
None of the shocks move the baseline path by a meaningful amount
body.explanation: The combined shock, which pushes r above g by shocking both variables together rather than one at a time, drove the debt ratio to nearly 99% of GDP after five years in this lesson's projection, far worse than any single shock applied on its own. This is the central lesson of stress-testing generally: a country's most dangerous scenario is rarely one variable moving in isolation, it is several plausible shocks compounding in the same window.

children.text: A Field Checklist for Monitoring India's Debt Sustainability Going Forward

body.title: Monitoring India's Debt Sustainability Going Forward
steps: Track the gap between India's effective interest rate and nominal GDP growth every quarter; a sustained narrowing toward zero, or a flip to r above g, is the single most important early signal from this course's entire framework
Watch for a repeat DISCOM-style crystallisation event, or a new one in a different sector, as the most plausible route for a contingent liability to add meaningfully to the debt stock quickly
Check the latest Article IV DSA's stress-test assumptions specifically, not just its headline risk rating, to see how severe a growth or rate shock it is actually assuming

Monitor whether India's rating outlook or CDS levels start moving toward the distress signals covered in Chapter 2, since the market's own pricing is currently far more benign than the adverse-scenario numbers
Revisit the FRBM Act's glide path progress against its FY2025-26 and ~2030-31 targets, and note whether any new escape clause has been invoked
Reassess this entire stress test periodically with updated r, g, and pb figures, since this lesson's numbers are illustrative and will drift from reality as conditions change

body.text: This lesson builds an illustrative stress test using approximate figures established earlier in this course, for educational purposes only. It is not investment advice, and it is not a forecast of India's actual debt path. Always verify current data against the latest RBI, Union Budget, and IMF Article IV publications before relying on a specific figure.

points: Under baseline assumptions (r near 7%, g near 9.6%, a modest primary deficit), India's general government debt-to-GDP ratio is on a gently declining path from roughly 82%, consistent with a favourable r-g gap

A combined growth-and-interest-rate shock pushes the ratio to nearly 99% of GDP after five years in this lesson's illustrative projection, closely echoing the IMF's own disputed 2024 adverse scenario, which was a disagreement about probability, not arithmetic

India's weak-but-positive fiscal reaction function and the FRBM Act's imperfect enforcement history mean discretionary or rule-based correction cannot be assumed to arrest a genuine adverse scenario automatically

The market's own signals, an upward-sloping yield curve, contained CDS, and a positive rating outlook, currently sit far closer to the baseline path than to any stress scenario, and are consistent with India's rupee-denominated, domestically-held debt structure

The real tail risk is not the headline ratio itself but several risks compounding at once, a sustained growth slowdown, a sustained rate shock, and a contingent liability crystallising in the same window, which is exactly what an investor or analyst should monitor rather than the ratio alone
